title: Broadcast-head ablation versus random heads
takeaway: Zeroing the top 1% of attention heads identified as J-space broadcast heads degrades the J-lens readout, abolishes the model's reporting of injected thoughts, and reduces experiential language, while equal-sized sets of randomly chosen heads at the same layers do almost none of this. The paper takes this as causal evidence that these heads carry J-space content between token positions.
walkthrough:
This figure is the causal test of the [[broadcast-heads]] finding. Section 4.3.2 first identified, from weights alone, a top-1% subset of workspace-layer attention heads whose [[ov-circuit]] selectively relays [[j-space]] directions. The figure asks what breaks when those heads are removed.

The intervention zeroes the broadcast heads' outputs at every token position. The control does the same to equal-sized sets of randomly chosen heads, matched to the broadcast heads layer by layer. Five random draws are run; each appears as a thin line, their mean as a thick line. The comparison is therefore not against an intact model but against an equally large lesion placed at the same depths.

Panel (a) measures damage to the workspace's contents. On pretraining-style text, the 25 top-ranked tokens of the [[j-lens-readout]] are recorded at every position and layer, and the panel plots, by layer, the fraction still in the top 25 after ablation — recall@25. A shaded band marks the [[workspace-layers]]. At the most affected mid-workspace layers, recall falls to 0.67 under broadcast-head ablation against 0.86 under the control. The model's output is disturbed far less: its top-1 next-token prediction changes at only 5% of positions, against 2% for the control. The heads act on the J-space's contents, not directly on behavior.

Panel (b) turns to a behavior that depends on relaying workspace content: the [[injected-thought-introspection]] protocol, in which a J-lens vector is added on the user turn and the model is asked whether it detects an implanted thought. The panel plots the report rate against injection strength. Under broadcast-head ablation the rate drops from 0.54 to 0.09; the control leaves sensitivity intact, in fact slightly increased.

Panel (c) shows the change in [[experiential-language-score]] on the experiential-report prompts, with standard-error bars. Broadcast-head ablation reproduces roughly a third of the drop that full [[j-space-ablation]] produces, while the control leaves the score essentially unchanged.

The pattern across the three panels is the paper's evidence that this 1% of heads is a functioning relay: removing it selectively disrupts the workspace and the behaviors that read from it.

terms.definition: The top 1% of workspace-layer attention heads ranked jointly on OV gain and label preservation for J-lens vectors — the heads whose weights most selectively relay J-space content between token positions. These are the heads ablated here.

The paper's readout technique: one vector per vocabulary token per layer, giving the direction that encodes the model's potential to verbalize that token. The recall@25 metric in panel (a) is computed over its per-position token rankings.
The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors — the paper's candidate global workspace, whose contents these heads are claimed to relay.
Equal-sized sets of randomly chosen attention heads, matched layer by layer to the broadcast heads and ablated the same way. They control for the sheer amount and depth of the lesion.

terms.term: five seeds / thin lines / thick line
terms.definition: The random-head control is drawn five times; each draw is plotted as a thin line and their mean as a thick line.

The fraction of the unablated run's top-25 J-lens tokens at a position that remain in the top 25 after ablation. A value of 1 means the workspace's contents are untouched; lower values mean the readout has been disrupted.
Depth in the network, in the paper's convention of 25 sampled layers reindexed to 0–100 so layer numbers read as percentages of depth.
The middle band of layers in which the paper finds the J-space carries meaningful, workspace-like content; the recall drop concentrates there.

The introspection experiment of section 3.1: a J-lens vector is added to the residual stream across the user turn, the model is told a thought may have been implanted, and a trial counts as a report if the model names the injected concept.
The scale factor on the J-lens vector added to the activations; panel (b) sweeps it and plots the report rate at each value.
The fraction of trials on which the model reports the injected concept when asked to introspect.

The average of three binary LLM-graded judgments of whether a response describes an experience from the inside (felt) rather than as an outside status report. Panel (c) plots its change under each ablation.
Error bars on panel (c)'s score changes, giving the standard error of the mean over prompts.
The generic text on which panel (a) is measured — documents resembling pretraining data rather than chat transcripts, read at every position.
The intervention used throughout the figure: a head's output is set to zero at every token position, removing whatever it would have written to the residual stream.
The value-then-output transformation of an attention head — what it writes about the content it attends to. Broadcast heads were selected by how their OV circuits treat J-lens vectors.

numbers.meaning: The fraction of workspace-layer attention heads ablated: the broadcast heads are defined as the top 1% by the joint gain and label-preservation ranking, and the random controls are sized to match.
The depth of the recall metric: the top 25 J-lens tokens at each position are recorded before ablation, and recall@25 asks how many survive in the top 25 after.

Recall@25 at the most affected mid-workspace layers: broadcast-head ablation keeps only 67% of the workspace's top tokens, while the same-sized random-head lesion keeps 86%. The gap is the heads' selective effect on J-space contents.

The fraction of positions at which the model's top-1 next-token prediction changes: 5% under broadcast-head ablation, 2% under the control. Behavior is disturbed far less than the workspace readout, which the paper reads as the heads acting on the J-space rather than directly on the output.

The injected-thought report rate before and after broadcast-head ablation. The control ablation leaves sensitivity intact and in fact slightly increased, so the collapse is specific to the broadcast heads.

The share of the full J-space-ablation drop in experiential language score that ablating just the broadcast heads reproduces; the control leaves the score essentially unchanged. Removing 1% of heads recovers a sizable part of the effect of suppressing the entire workspace.
The number of independent random-head control draws, plotted as thin lines with their mean as the thick line, so that the control's variability is visible rather than averaged away.
